video_clips.summary: A presentation highlights officers who swiftly lifted and carried a woman in distress out of her home, showcasing the department's dedication to going 'above and beyond the call of duty.' This moment resonates with residents' desire for safe, compassionate policing.

video_clips.section_title: Mayfield Small Area Plan Adoption & Anti-Displacement Commitment
video_clips.summary: Council adopts the Mayfield Small Area Plan with a critical amendment: they commit to tracking median income and housing values to prevent displacement. This addresses the community's fear that revitalization will erase the historic Black neighborhood, ensuring current residents can stay and benefit.

video_clips.section_title: Architectural Review Board Affirmation: Caroline Street Wall Removal
video_clips.summary: Council votes 7-0 to affirm the ARB's decision to allow the removal of a historic 12-inch retaining wall on Lower Caroline Street for a new driveway. A council member notes the procedural tension, while the vote signals a prioritization of private property rights over streetscape integrity in this specific waiver case.

video_clips.section_title: Zoning Code Update for Faith & Nonprofit Institutions
video_clips.summary: Council unanimously passes an ordinance updating local zoning to align with state law, allowing religious and nonprofit organizations to build taller structures (up to 45 feet) and include non-residential facilities like shelters. This removes barriers for faith-based groups providing community services.

During the annual retreat portion of the meeting, EDA members centered their discussion around five strategic
themes: business climate, marketing/tourism, public perception, retail/workforce support, and future redevelopment.
A central goal of the retreat was to move away from purely ideation-based discussions toward a methodical, project-
oriented planning process. To ensure accountability, the chair assigned specific board members as "sponsors" to lead
each initiative, with all action items categorized by 30, 60, and 90 day execution windows to ensure measurable
In the area of business climate, the board identified the need to analyze the current Business, Professional, and
Occupational License (BPOL) tax structure. Members requested a revenue breakdown by tier to evaluate how these
taxes affect the attraction of professional services and defense contractors, with an intent to approach City Council
with evidence-based solutions rather than just feedback during future City Relations meetings. Regarding Marketing
and Tourism, the members proposed a new, EDA-specific social media presence focused on "living and working" in
Fredericksburg, distinguishing it from existing tourism-focused outlets, and discussed potential influencer-led
campaigns. EDA members expressed a strong interest in ensuring these efforts are tied to clear return-on-investment

video_clips.summary: Coming from a joint session with the School Board, council and Planning Commission members discuss the Area 10 small area plan's focus on walkability along Lafayette Boulevard and access to the two elementary schools there. Staff describe the planned Cortland Drive Connector, now in engineering procurement, with construction expected around 2028 through Safe Routes to School.

Asked about pre-approved housing plans, planning staff say infill homes typically go in at about 150% the size of their neighbors and keep getting more expensive. They describe pre-approved plans, designs the city approves in advance for homes from single-family to small multiplexes, as a 'carrot' that makes permitting faster and cheaper.

Councilor McIntosh, joining by phone, says state security rules have given cannabis shops elsewhere a 'highly fortified look' with thick plexiglass and bars, and asks what the city can do locally, especially downtown. Staff say the state is still writing those regulations and outline camera, alarm and back-room storage requirements.

Staff recommend raising the penalty for a third or later nuisance violation, such as tall grass, trash and exterior clutter, to $500, aimed at repeat offenders they say are mostly out-of-state owners. Members weigh neighbors' frustration against hardship cases, and Vice Mayor Frye calls $500 steep.
